turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's a pleasure to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello Dr. Smith. It’s nice to meet you too. I, uh, I guess I’m here because... well, it’s a bit embarrassing to admit, honestly. I spend a lot of my time down at the local art museum—since I'm not working anymore, it gives me something good to do, you know, gets me out of the house and keeps me involved in the community. We have this big event we do, the art walk, and there's always a whole lot of planning and coordinating that goes into it with the other folks there. 

But what brings me in today is that... well, people at the museum will be talking right to me about the next art walk, going over the details or who is setting up what, and I’ll be looking right at them. I mean, I'm making eye contact, I'm nodding, I'm giving them my full physical attention. But then, all of a sudden, I’ll realize I completely missed the entire middle part of what they just said. It’s like my brain just takes a little vacation right in the middle of their sentence. And then I have to awkwardly stop them and ask them to run it by me all over again. It happens so much, and they must think I'm just being rude or that I don't care about the art walk, but I really am trying to listen! It’s just getting incredibly frustrating to have to constantly ask people to repeat themselves when they're standing two feet away from me.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly describes looking right at people when they are talking but realizing they completely missed the middle of what was said, requiring them to ask for it to be repeated.

turns.doctor_question: When your mind takes these 'vacations,' do you ever experience any unusual physical sensations, like a sudden twitching, staring blankly without being able to respond, or feeling like your body is doing something on its own?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, definitely nothing like that. Goodness, no. It’s not like a... a spasm or a fit, or anything where I lose control of my body. My body is right there, doing exactly what it's supposed to do. If I'm holding a cup of coffee, I don't drop it. I can still take a sip, I can still nod my head, smile, shift my weight... I'm completely in control physically. 

In fact, I think that's the whole reason it's so embarrassing! I look so completely normal and engaged that nobody has any clue I'm a million miles away. Like just last Tuesday, Mary—she's the one who organizes the local watercolor artists for the museum—she was standing right in front of me, and I was nodding along, completely physically normal. No staring blankly like a zombie where I can't respond, I was looking right in her eyes, making all the right 'uh-huh' noises. 

But my mind? My mind had just... wandered off to think about whether I remembered to put the trash bins out on the curb. Because the garbage truck comes real early on Wednesdays in my neighborhood, usually around 6 AM, and if I don't put them out the night before, I end up having to chase the truck down the street in my slippers, which I've done more times than I care to admit at my age. So, no, physically I'm fine, no twitching or anything weird. It's purely just my thoughts that go taking a stroll without my permission, leaving my body behind to pretend it's still paying attention.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes their mind wandering off and being 'a million miles away' while someone is speaking directly to them, merely pretending to pay attention.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes their thoughts frequently 'go taking a stroll without my permission,' indicating distractibility by unrelated internal thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient admits to frequently forgetting the daily chore of putting the trash bins out, resulting in having to chase the garbage truck.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient explicitly denies any loss of physical control, spasms, or staring blankly without being able to respond.

turns.doctor_question: Does this same 'mind wandering' happen to you when you are by yourself, for example, when you are reading a book or watching television at home?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. It’s not just a social thing, it happens when it's just me and the quiet house, too. It’s funny you mention reading, because... well, I’ll sit down in my favorite armchair—the one right by the front window where the natural light is best in the afternoons, it's a great spot—and I'll have a gallery packet for the museum, or maybe a set of notes from our last planning committee meeting. I always want to make sure I'm prepared, you know, to pull my weight with the group, so I try to be really thorough with the materials they give us. 

And I’ll start out just fine. I’m reading the first page, taking it all in, understanding the scheduling for the volunteers or the layout for the new exhibits. But then, after just a few minutes... it's the most frustrating thing. My eyes will keep right on moving over the page, tracking the lines of text perfectly. I'll even physically turn the page! But my mind has completely wandered off somewhere else entirely. I'll be thinking about whether I need to go to the store to buy more of those little cocktail napkins for the reception, or if the hardware store has the right kind of picture wire on sale, or if it's going to rain on Thursday and ruin the outdoor displays. 

And then I'll suddenly snap back to reality and realize I haven't absorbed a single word of what was in front of me. I have to go all the way back and read the exact same part all over again. Sometimes I have to read the same paragraph three or four times before the meaning actually registers in my brain. It makes getting through a simple ten-page packet take half the afternoon! 

And television is exactly the same way. I'll put on a history program or the evening news, thinking I'll relax and learn something, and I'll be staring right at the screen. But ten minutes will go by and I'll realize I haven't heard a single thing the narrator said because I was busy thinking about the gutters needing cleaning. It's just a constant, endless cycle of having to rewind the TV or re-read my notes just to catch up on what I was supposed to be paying attention to in the first place.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a clear inability to sustain attention during tasks like reading or watching television, noting that their mind wanders after just a few minutes and they have to re-read or rewind to understand the material.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly mentions being distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as buying cocktail napkins, picture wire, or cleaning the gutters, while trying to focus on reading or watching TV.

turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced this type of difficulty staying focused on tasks throughout most of your life, or is this a problem that has only started more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, when you put it like that, it’s funny because... I’ve been thinking about this a lot lately, especially since I started spending so much time at the museum and noticing how much trouble I have with those gallery packets. And honestly? It’s not new. It’s really not. I mean, I’m 63 now, and I’ve been out of the workforce for a bit, but if I really sit back and think about it, this has been happening for as long as I can remember. 

I was actually going through some old boxes up in the attic a few months ago—I was looking for this old set of watercolor brushes I used to have, thinking I might try my hand at it again, you know, since I’m around all these artists now. I never did find the brushes, but I found this old cedar chest my mother kept. And inside, she had saved all these things from when I was a boy. My old report cards from grade school were in there. I sat on the floor up there for over an hour just reading through them. 

And, oh boy, let me tell you, it was like reading about the exact same person sitting in front of you today. Every single year, third grade, fourth grade, fifth grade... the teachers would write these little notes in the margins. "Daydreams during lessons." "Needs constant reminders to finish his work." "Stares out the window instead of completing his spelling tests." It was just page after page of that. 

And it brought back all these memories of sitting at the kitchen table—we had this yellow Formica table with the metal edges, you know the kind?—and my mother would have to sit right there beside me. Every single night. Just to get me through a worksheet on fractions or a reading assignment. If she got up to stir the soup on the stove or answer the telephone, my mind would just drift right off, and I’d start playing with my pencil or looking at the pattern on the linoleum floor. She had to sit there and tap the paper and say, "Focus, focus," just to keep me on track. And this was all way before I was even twelve years old. So, no, it’s not a recent problem at all. It’s like my brain has just always preferred to be somewhere else, even way back then. It's just... well, it's just getting harder to hide it now that I'm trying to coordinate things with other adults who expect me to be on the ball, you know?

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a lifelong history of his mind drifting off during tasks, daydreaming during lessons, and needing his mother to keep him focused on homework.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient recalls that his childhood report cards stated he needed constant reminders to finish his work and would fail to complete his spelling tests.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes that as a child, if his mother stepped away, he would immediately become distracted by extraneous things like his pencil or the pattern on the floor.
